name: GraphQL
vendor: GraphQL Foundation (Linux Foundation), created at Facebook
license: Specification: Open Web Foundation Agreement 1.0 since September 2017; GraphQL.js reference implementation: MIT since September 2017 (BSD plus a patent grant before)
summary: A query language and runtime for APIs: the server publishes a typed schema, and each client asks one endpoint for exactly the fields it needs.
intro: A GraphQL service publishes a schema written in GraphQL’s type language: object types with typed fields, such as an `Order` with a `status` and a `customer`, plus root types listing the entry points for queries (reads), mutations (writes) and subscriptions (streams of events). Clients send a document to one endpoint, conventionally `POST /graphql` with a JSON body holding the query and its variables. The server parses the document and validates it against the schema before running anything, then executes it. Every field is backed by a resolver, a function that gets its parent object and the field’s arguments and returns a value from a database, another service or memory. Query fields may resolve in parallel; the top-level fields of a mutation run one after another. The response is JSON with the data under `data`, shaped exactly like the query, and any problems under `errors`, so one response can carry partial data and errors together. The schema can itself be queried (introspection), which powers editors such as GraphiQL, code generators and typed clients.

The specification defines the language, type system, validation and execution, and deliberately leaves out transport and storage. HTTP with JSON is the usual pairing, described by a separate GraphQL over HTTP specification that is still a draft; subscriptions usually run over WebSockets or server-sent events. GraphQL.js is the reference implementation (v17 shipped in June 2026), and there are servers for most languages, such as Apollo Server, GraphQL Yoga, graphql-java and Strawberry, plus engines that generate a schema from a database. The GraphQL Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, publishes the spec in dated editions; the September 2025 edition, the first since October 2021, added OneOf input objects and schema coordinates. Using GraphQL costs nothing; managed services such as AWS AppSync charge per operation.
strengths: Each client asks for exactly the fields it needs, across related objects, in one request: fewer round trips and smaller payloads on mobile networks
A typed schema: queries are validated before they run, and introspection drives GraphiQL, code generation and typed clients
Evolves without version numbers: new fields don’t affect existing queries, and old ones are marked `@deprecated` while they keep working
One endpoint over many backends: resolvers can call databases, REST APIs and gRPC services, so a GraphQL layer can unify existing systems
Subscriptions use the same schema and query language as reads, for real-time updates
limits: HTTP caching is harder: requests are usually `POST`s to one URL, which browsers and CDNs don’t cache. You need `GET` with persisted queries, or client-side caches keyed by globally unique object IDs
The N+1 problem: naive resolvers make one backend call per item in a list, so 50 orders can mean 50 customer lookups. Batching with a tool like DataLoader is effectively required

Clients write the queries, so a deep or wide one can overload the server. Public APIs need depth limits, cost analysis or rate limits by cost; GitHub charges points per query, 5,000 an hour per user, and requires a page size on every list
Errors don’t map to HTTP status codes: a response with partial data comes back as `200` with an `errors` list, so monitoring by status code misses failures
File uploads aren’t in the spec: servers adopt a community multipart convention, and graphql.org recommends uploading through signed URLs instead

snippet.title: A GraphQL Yoga server with resolvers and DataLoader batching
source: // npm install graphql graphql-yoga dataloader pg
const db = new pg.Pool(); // connection settings from PGHOST, PGUSER, PGDATABASE...
order: async (_: unknown, { id }: { id: string }) =>
(await db.query("SELECT id, status, customer_id FROM orders WHERE id = $1", [id])).rows[0] ?? null,
recentOrders: async (_: unknown, { first }: { first: number }) =>
(await db.query("SELECT id, status, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1", [Math.min(first, 100)])).rows,
// Runs once per order; the loader turns 20 calls into one query (no N+1)
customer: (order: { customer_id: string }, _: unknown, ctx: { customers: DataLoader<string, unknown> }) =>
// A fresh loader per request, so batches and its cache never mix users
const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE id = ANY($1)", [ids]);
return ids.map((id) => rows.find((row) => row.id === id) ?? null);
// Client: { recentOrders(first: 20) { id status customer { name } } }

sections.title: REST, GraphQL and gRPC
sections.intro: All three run over HTTP, but they put the contract, and the choice of what comes back, in different places.

rows.label: Contract
values: A schema, required; clients can query it

rows.label: Encoding
values: Usually JSON; the spec doesn’t require one

rows.label: HTTP caching
values: Only with `GET` or persisted queries; otherwise client-side caches

rows.label: Errors
values: An `errors` list in the body, often with status `200`

rows.label: Real-time
values: Subscriptions; the transport is left to the implementation

rows.label: From a browser
values: Only through gRPC-Web and a proxy

sections.title: Ways to run a GraphQL API
sections.intro: You can write resolvers yourself, generate the schema from a database, or rent a managed service. AWS list prices checked October 6, 2026.

items.name: GraphQL.js
items.text: The JavaScript reference implementation maintained by the GraphQL Foundation; v17 shipped in June 2026. Many Node servers build on it.

items.name: Apollo Server and GraphQL Yoga
items.text: Full HTTP servers around GraphQL.js. Other languages have their own: graphql-java, Strawberry for Python and more.

items.name: Hasura, PostGraphile, pg_graphql
items.text: Build a GraphQL schema from an existing database. pg_graphql runs inside PostgreSQL as an extension and is called through one SQL function, `graphql.resolve`.

items.name: AWS AppSync
items.text: Resolvers connect fields to DynamoDB, Lambda, OpenSearch, RDS, EventBridge or HTTP endpoints. $4.00 per million queries and mutations, $2.00 per million real-time updates, $0.08 per million connection-minutes.

items.name: Azure API Management
items.text: Passes GraphQL through to an existing server, or builds a synthetic GraphQL API from a schema with resolvers that call HTTP backends.

items.name: Firebase Data Connect
items.text: Google’s managed GraphQL API over Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, with generated, type-safe SDKs for web and mobile apps.

story: In 2012 Facebook began rebuilding its iOS and Android apps, which until then were thin wrappers around the mobile website and often slow and crash-prone. Native apps needed News Feed as data, not HTML. The team looked at RESTful resources and FQL, Facebook’s SQL-like API, and was frustrated by the gap between the data the apps wanted and the server queries they had to make. A few engineers started the project that became GraphQL, and a native iOS News Feed built on it shipped that year.

Facebook released a working draft of the spec and GraphQL.js as a “technical preview” in July 2015, after the excitement around Relay, its GraphQL-based app framework. By then GraphQL served hundreds of billions of API calls a day inside Facebook. In September 2016 it dropped the preview label, the day GitHub announced the first major public GraphQL API.

In September 2017 Facebook relicensed the spec under the Open Web Foundation Agreement and GraphQL.js under MIT, dropping the separate patent grant that had come with its BSD licence. In November 2018 the Linux Foundation announced a GraphQL Foundation with members including Airbnb, Apollo, GitHub, Shopify and Twitter, and from March 2019 the spec has been developed under the Joint Development Foundation.

choices.why: Facebook already had feed ranking, storage and business logic. So each field is backed by a function that can call any existing code, and GraphQL provides no storage of its own.
A query follows relationships between objects in one request, where a RESTful service might need several round trips, which are expensive on mobile networks. The response mirrors the query.

Typed fields let the server reject bad queries with clear errors before running them and suited the typed Objective-C and Java apps. Because the schema can be queried, tools like GraphiQL and Relay can build on it.

The client’s query decides the shape of the data, so new fields don’t affect existing clients and old ones can be deprecated but keep working. In 2015 Facebook said it still supported three years of app releases on one version of its API.
